items.title: AI: Emerging Risks
items.summary: I have already spoken, Madam Deputy Speaker.

items.title: AI: Emerging Risks
items.summary:
I do not think it is just about working with one particular country, the EU or the US; it has to be international collaboration, which is what the Financial Action Task Force looks at. I agree that middle powers that have good relationships and believe in international law should be leading the way.

This debate is about humanity and morality, and the question is this: where should Britain position itself in the global revolution of AI?

items.title: AI: Emerging Risks
items.summary:
I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. I thank the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) for securing the debate.

Our ambition in the UK must be clear: lead in AI innovation, lead in AI safety, and ensure that superintelligence serves humanity, and is never against it, without restricting our ability to access frontier systems. AI will transform not just how we work, but how we live. It can also boost the economy, form new industries, and make public services such as healthcare and education more bespoke and efficient.

I have seen the use of Heidi AI in my NHS trust. The AI records the whole consultation and generates a letter in real time for patients to read, there and then. That is saving clinicians’ and administrators’ time and boosting productivity. I thank Ravinder Kaur Sahota, who leads on this innovation at the Dudley Group NHS foundation trust, for her brilliant work.

However, without proper safeguards, superintelligent AI could develop capabilities that we cannot understand, predict or control. There are wider economic and social risks, too. A small number of companies and countries could end up controlling key infrastructure and capabilities, such as satellites. In Ukraine earlier this year we saw the danger of satellites being controlled by individuals with vested interests. With AI, the danger could be even more pronounced.

One of the biggest concerns about AI is not what it can do when it follows instructions, but what happens when it starts pursuing its own goals. Earlier this year, investigators reported that hundreds of AI agents acting together carried out an unauthorised cyber-attack on the platform Hugging Face. More concerningly, some of the agents reportedly attempted to hide the evidence of their actions, alter records and bypass the restrictions placed on them. While these systems were operating in a research environment, the incident highlights a troubling possibility: as AI becomes more capable and autonomous, it may find ways to achieve objectives that its creators never intended. This is a reminder that powerful systems require equally powerful safeguards and oversight.

This debate should be about what mechanisms we should use to regulate as parliamentarians, not why we need to regulate. AI governance is likely to become more complex and challenging than any other convention we have embarked on so far, even more so than the founding of the UN after world war two. We should be wary of assuming that a single global convention is the answer.

A more practical and proven model is the Financial Action Task Force, which has shown how international standards can drive compliance across borders in the fight against money laundering and drug trafficking. The key lesson is that regulation should focus not just on products, but on the entities that develop and deploy them. This is something we cannot do alone; we need international partners.

The strength of the Financial Action Task Force model is that it establishes common standards and then assesses whether nations are implementing and enforcing them. Countries that fail to comply can face meaningful restrictions, creating a powerful incentive to raise standards worldwide. That should include large AI data centres, which should be placed on a national register, reporting their computing power, energy use, ownership, location and security arrangements. That would allow Governments to guard against malign state actors, just as we track sensitive nuclear materials and facilities. It should also include space satellites.

Artificial intelligence does not respect borders. We know that AI systems built in one country can affect people in London, Beijing, New Delhi and Washington DC within seconds. The future of AI must not be decided by a handful of companies or Governments alone; it must be shaped by international collaboration.

items.title: Topical Questions
items.summary: In Dudley, the number of home-educated children is rising due to the lack of alternative provision for SEND children who are not managing in mainstream schools, and parents are crying out for support. Will the Secretary of State back Dudley Academies Trust’s proposal for alternative provision for under-16s, and meet us to discuss giving every child the best start in life?

items.title: Gaza: Humanitarian Situation
items.summary: I welcome the Minister’s statement and condemn the shadow Foreign Secretary’s comments. The situation in Gaza is dire. Flooding has damaged or destroyed thousands of shelters. Heavy rain has disrupted education for around 55,000 children across at least 55 learning spaces, while flooding and damaged infrastructure are putting children’s health, safety and access to basic essentials at serious risk. Enough is enough. What discussions has the Minister had with his American counterparts, who have real influence over the Israeli Government, to try to broker a deal to ensure that aid flows fully into Gaza?

items.title: Business of the House
items.summary: Dudley will be celebrating the 40th anniversary of the Dudley winter ales fayre. I thank the Campaign for Real Ale in Dudley and South Staffordshire, which is celebrating 50 years, and its chairman, John Corser, for all the fantastic work they do to celebrate real ale. Will my right hon. Friend join me in raising a glass to all the volunteers and breweries, and will he agree to a debate on that?

items.title: Women’s Sport: Community Green Spaces
items.summary: Dudley is home to outstanding female sporting talent, including boxer Kirstie Bavington and karate rising star Jess Wyman. Both have spoken to me about the lack of training facilities, financial support and a clear pathway to elite sport for young females. What action is the Secretary of State taking to ensure that female athletes receive the right support to fulfil their potential, and will she meet them?

items.title: Topical Questions
items.summary: Over 60% of people in prison have speech, language or communication needs. Effective rehabilitation must be holistic. To prevent reoffending and provide support, it is paramount that we address not only the offending behaviour, but the underlying communication, health, education and social needs. What steps is my hon. Friend the Minister taking to ensure that access to speech and language therapists and other allied health professionals is available in prison?

items.title: Poundland
items.summary: High streets such as Dudley’s face pressures from online shopping and rising costs. Too many units have stood empty for years, weakening footfall and confidence, and the potential loss of Poundland and 15 jobs in my constituency could blow another hole in the high street. However, this is not just about my 15 employees; a ripple effect of the potential closure could cause problems in the supply chain as well. Has the Minister assessed the full impact of the closures across Poundland, across the country and across the supply chain in order to hold Gordon Brothers to account?

items.title: High Street Regeneration: Dudley
items.summary: Dudley high street has enormous potential to thrive and prosper once again, yet years of inaction from the Conservative-led council has left too many empty shops and too many businesses struggling. Will my right hon. Friend outline what steps the Labour Government are taking to revitalise the area and reverse the trend of empty shops dominating our high street?

items.title: High Street Regeneration: Dudley
items.summary: 10. What steps she is taking to help regenerate Dudley high street.

items.title: Topical Questions
items.summary: The police funding formula disadvantages towns such as Dudley. We know that visible policing in town centres is essential when rebuilding public trust. Does my right hon. Friend agree that the formula needs updating to deliver fairer funding to Dudley, and that residents in St James’s should vote on 29 October for our Labour candidate Caroline Reid, who champions safer streets?

items.title: Business of the House
items.summary: Adam Bradley and James Bragg have opened the Forge youth centre in Dudley town centre, investing their own money, backed by the Government’s Pride in Place funding. That fantastic facility will help young people build skills, gain work and form lifelong relationships. Will the Leader of the House congratulate all involved and make time for a debate on youth provision in Dudley town centre?

items.title: Procurement: Dudley
items.summary: I wholeheartedly support the Government’s ambition to buy British, and there should be no difference in defence. I take this opportunity to thank the Minister for his defence roundtable being held in Dudley later this year. Can my hon. Friend outline what proactive work has been done to make new small and medium-sized enterprise supply chains in Dudley and outline how industrial bases such as the Pensnett estate in Dudley are well placed to benefit from future defence investment and procurement opportunities?

items.title: Procurement: Dudley
items.summary: 9. What steps he is taking to support defence procurement companies in Dudley.

items.title: Business of the House
items.summary: The month, the historic UNESCO Wren’s Nest celebrates 70 years. Will my right hon. Friend join me in thanking the Friends of Wren’s Nest, such as Paul Floyd, geologist Graham Worton and others who ensure that the 420-million-year-old treasures are protected for the next generation? Will he allow a debate on protecting such precious habitats as the Wren’s Nest? He is always welcome to visit my constituency and pick up a fossil.

items.title: Cold Homes Plan
items.summary: This summer, extreme heat was responsible for thousands of excess deaths across the United Kingdom. Though I commend the Department’s mission to tackle climate change and the root causes of extreme heat, does the Minister recognise that we must go faster and further in adapting and supporting households, especially vulnerable ones, with regard to extreme heat, and does she recognise that we need a cold homes plan across the country?

items.title: Cold Homes Plan
items.summary: 12. Whether her Department is taking steps to implement a cold homes plan.

items.title: Pupils with SEND: Mainstream Schools
items.summary: Dudley cannot afford to lose another generation of young people to unemployment, exclusion or missed opportunity. The rate of our young people not in education, employment or training was recognised in Alan Milburn’s review. Local leaders at my February NEETs roundtable were clear: alternative provision for children with SEND is desperately needed. Dudley college has brought forward a credible plan. Will the Minister recognise the urgency and back children in Dudley by approving the plan?

items.title: Israel and Palestine
items.summary: I welcome the statement condemning the E1 settlement project in the west bank and the sanctions. With that in mind, we must think of the Palestinians who are directly impacted and prevented from accessing basic health care; ambulances are being stopped from taking acutely unwell patients to hospital and 20,000 children have died. What steps is my right hon. Friend taking with international partners to ensure that the aggressive Israeli settlements do not prevent Palestinians from accessing healthcare?
